source.title: A Precise Performance Analysis of Support Vector Regression
source.authors: Houssem Sifaou; A. Kammoun; Mohamed-Slim Alouini

record.tranche_reason: Analyzes sample-size-dependent test risk in hard and soft support vector regression, using an asymptotic analysis and numerical illustrations rather than the original deep-network experiments.
record.gate_note: The paper reports test-risk curves over sample-to-feature ratio δ, parameter sensitivity, and results under impulsive noise. Results it cites from other work are not recorded as rows. The impulsive-noise comparison concerns robustness, not whether the double-descent peak is caused by noise, so it is summarized under fits_no_version.
record.test_reason: The paper derives asymptotic and finite-sample (p=200) test risk of hard and soft SVR as the sample ratio δ=n/p varies. It shows sample-wise non-monotonic risk under fixed parameters, which disappears under optimal ε or C. This is a new model class (linear SVR) with results on V3 and on the regularization part of V6, so T3 fits better than T2.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. Arbitrary SVR parameters can yield non-monotonic sample-wise risk, so more samples can hurt; optimally tuned H-SVR and S-SVR give decreasing risk. The authors state this is consistent with linear-regression and neural-network findings. They also conclude that optimally regularized S-SVR is more robust to outliers than ridge.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses asymptotic high-dimensional analysis and numerical risk curves for hard and soft support vector regression, rather than deep-network size, epoch, or sample sweeps.
record.method_sensitivity: Risk depends on the SVR tolerance ε and regularization constant C; the reported sample-wise non-monotonicity can be mitigated by optimizing these parameters. H-SVR risk also varies with signal power β.

fits_no_version.finding: Under impulsive (Student-type) noise, optimally tuned H-SVR approaches the null estimator's risk at d=3. Optimally tuned S-SVR is slightly worse than optimal ridge under mild impulsive noise but much better under highly impulsive noise (Fig. 8).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Optimally tuned soft SVR is more robust to impulsive noise in test risk than optimally tuned ridge regression, while hard SVR degrades toward the null estimator.

record.problems: The central curves are asymptotic theoretical predictions with finite-sample illustrations at p=200; the figures do not provide uncertainty estimates. The study concerns a high-dimensional linear data model and SVR, not deep networks. Several curve values are only available in figures.
record.rows_left_out: No reported result directly measuring noise as a cause of the double-descent peak was extracted. The impulsive-noise robustness comparison in Section IV.C/Figure 8 is summarized under fits_no_version because it compares robustness rather than peak formation or shape.

untested.parts: Deep networks; any model-size interaction. The tested threshold is the H-SVR feasibility boundary δ⋆, not interpolation of training data in the usual sense.
Whether label noise or variance drives the peak; triple or multiple descent. The impulsive-noise experiment uses only optimally tuned estimators and does not address peak formation.

missing.what: H-SVR risk vs δ for fixed ε∈{1,1.2,1.5} alongside optimal ε (σ=1, β=1). This shows the fixed-ε curves are non-monotonic, with risk rising, over a range extending to δ=5.

record.verdict_notes: The V6 limits_scope label on r5–r6 was dropped: those rows are not linked to V6, and the fixed-C cusps bear on V3. The peak occurs at the H-SVR feasibility threshold δ⋆ (>1, set by ε and σ), an analogue of the interpolation threshold rather than the same thing. Results are mostly figure-only, with no uncertainty reported. Neither original source is this study.

versions.untested_parts: Model-size double descent in deep networks.
The evidence concerns sample-wise test risk in high-dimensional linear SVR, not deep-network models generally.
Capacity-wise curves across model classes and the classical U-shaped curve.
Whether a single effective-complexity measure predicts peak location across size, epochs, and sample count.

Whether label noise or variance causes the peak; whether multiple peaks occur; the paper tests parameter tuning and reports risk under impulsive noise, but does not establish a noise-driven peak mechanism.
Whether measuring complexity by an effective parameter count turns second descent into an ordinary U-shaped curve.

relationships.reason: Risk rises with more samples. For β=0.5 it rises throughout (r1). For β=1,2 it rises after a minimum toward δ⋆ (r2–r3). S-SVR shows a cusp near δ⋆ that sharpens with C (r5–r6).
relationships.display_finding: Risk rose throughout for β = 0.5 and after a minimum toward δ⋆ for β = 1 or 2; S-SVR's cusp near δ⋆ sharpened with C.
